html:
A great mosque in Kairouan, Tunisia, first founded in 670 by the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi together with the city itself. It is one of the oldest and most important mosques in North Africa.

Kairouan was the Arab base for the conquest of the Maghreb, built inland, away from the coast where the Byzantine fleet could strike. The first mosque was simple and was rebuilt several times. Most of what stands now dates from the 9th century under the Aghlabid emirs, who ruled the province for the Abbasid caliphs.

Its massive square minaret, built in the 8th or 9th century, is among the oldest minarets still standing anywhere. The prayer hall rests on hundreds of marble and granite columns taken from Roman and Byzantine ruins. The mihrab, the niche facing Mecca, is framed with glazed lustre tiles from Iraq and carved marble panels. The mosque became a model for later mosques across the Maghreb and al-Andalus, and Kairouan grew into a centre of Islamic learning in the west, alongside later al-Qarawiyyin in Fez.
